name: Earlobe reduction/repair
lead: Earlobe repair and reduction are minor plastic-surgery procedures that reshape or mend the earlobe. Repair restores a lobe that has been torn or split, often by heavy earrings, snagged jewelry, trauma or long-term stretched piercings, so that the lobe looks intact and can be repierced if the person wishes. Reduction addresses oversized or protruding lobes, bringing the lower ear into better proportion with the rest of the ear and face.[1][2][3]

For appearance, the procedures work directly on a visible feature: a closed, smooth lobe edge replaces a cleft or enlarged hole, and a smaller or better-positioned lobe changes how the ear reads in profile and from the front. The published literature consists largely of surgical technique papers describing Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap and double-flap closures, all designed to avoid notching of the lobe edge, along with small retrospective series.[4][5][6][7][8] A paper on cosmetic repair notes that piercing-related complications are rising with the popularity of body piercing.[3]

The topic sits at the meeting point of body-modification culture and cosmetic surgery. Ear piercing is among the oldest forms of body modification, ear stretching spread in Western subcultures in the 1990s, and surgical repair is described as the only reliable way to fully close a heavily stretched lobe.[12][13]

sections.h: Anatomy and why lobes tear or enlarge
paras: The earlobe is the soft lower part of the outer ear, made of connective tissue rather than cartilage, with a rich blood supply and many nerve endings. Wikipedia notes it has no major known biological function, and that lobes range continuously from attached to free rather than falling into two types.[11]

Earlobe piercing is common across cultures and eras, and Wikipedia's earring article notes that a lobe can only carry so much weight before a piercing tears; heavy earrings worn for long periods can stretch the hole, and sports or snagging can cause a split. In one study it cites, about 2.5 percent of people with pierced ears had traumatic tearing, and torn lobes may need surgical repair.[13] A 2005 review cited on the same page found complications in up to 35 percent of people with pierced ears, of which infection, allergy, keloid and tearing were the reported categories.[13]

Deliberate stretching enlarges a healed piercing in small steps to hold larger jewelry, and the lobe is the most commonly stretched site. Wikipedia describes risks such as blowouts and tears from rapid stretching, says a stretched hole may shrink after jewelry is removed but results vary, and states that surgical repair is the only reliable way to fully close a stretched lobe.[12]

Wikipedia notes that torn lobes may be sutured and cleft lobes usually need a tissue graft.[1] Published techniques include a half Z-plasty,[5] an L-plasty series of 9 cleft-earlobe patients in which one repair had slight notching,[6] a V-flap alternative to Z-plasty described in 1984,[7] a double-flap technique,[8] and L-specular and double-round plasty.[9] A guidewire punch technique has been described to remove unwanted epithelial tracts left by piercings.[10] One author outlines 11 surgical pearls and describes immediate repiercing.[3]

Other reviews and reports in the literature include a 2004 review titled Repair of the torn earlobe, a 2002 Otolaryngologic Clinics article on torn earlobe repair, and a 1994 British Journal of Plastic Surgery paper on split earlobe repair, reflecting how long the problem has been addressed by surgeons.[4][15][16]

The common principle across designs is to excise the epithelialised edges of the cleft and close the lobe in layers, using a flap so that the final scar does not run straight along the lobe's edge, which is where notching arises. The V-flap paper describes the technique as easier than Z-plasty while serving the same purpose of preventing notching at the rim.[7]

Wikipedia calls lobe repositioning the hardest part of otoplasty and describes the Gosain technique and other methods to pull a protruding lobe toward the head. It says protrusion can stem from connective tissue linking the lobe to the helical tail, the shape of the concha or the density of fibres within the lobe, and that if the upper ear is set back while the lobe still sticks out, the ear looks disproportionate.[1] Grokipedia describes excising a wedge or a few millimeters of fat and skin for a protruding lobule.[2]

Otoplasty more generally has a long history: Wikipedia traces ear surgery to the Sushruta Samhita, describes Johann Friedrich Dieffenbach's 1845 approach to prominent ears, an 1881 ear-pinning operation by Edward Talbott Ely in New York, and the Mustarde and Stenstrom techniques of 1963, and says more than 170 procedures are now recognised.[1]

sections.h: What the procedure involves in general terms
paras: Wikipedia states that many ear procedures are outpatient and may use local anesthesia, local with sedation, or general anesthesia depending on the case and age. For ear pinning it describes swelling and bruising that usually fade within about two weeks and a headband worn at night for several weeks.[1] Lobe-only procedures are smaller than full otoplasty, and individual surgeons' protocols for dressings, suture removal and repiercing timing differ between the published papers.[3][5]

Technique papers focus on notching of the rim, the outcome closures are built to prevent; in the 1990 L-plasty series, both simple repairs had moderate notching along the lower lobe border and one of nine L-plasty repairs had slight notching.[6] Otoplasty in general carries risks Wikipedia lists as hematoma, infection, suture extrusion with granuloma and overcorrection.[1]

People prone to keloids may form raised scars at lobe piercings and incisions. Wikipedia reports that ear piercings are among the most common keloid sites, that excision alone has a reported 70 to 100 percent recurrence rate, and that combination approaches lower recurrence; it identifies people with sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latin American ancestry and those with a family history as more commonly affected.[14]

Studies are small retrospective series and technique reports. A retrospective study of 9 patients with 11 cleft earlobe repairs, mean follow-up 5.5 months, found moderate notching in both simple repairs and slight notching in 1 of 9 L-plasty repairs, with no complications.[6] Other publications describe half Z-plasty, V-flap, double-flap and specular techniques.[5][7][8][9] No randomized trials were found.

Related procedures include full otoplasty for prominent ears, keloid treatment after piercing, and dermal punching or scalpeling in the body-modification community, where Wikipedia describes the latter as enlarging or repositioning a hole.[1][12][14] Ear stretching itself has ancient precedent, appearing in ancient Egypt, with the Iceman Otzi, and in various African, Asian and Indigenous American cultures.[12]

lore.intro: Earlobe repair is discussed mainly in surgical and piercing contexts rather than as a looksmaxxing theme, so most claims below come from the technique and body-modification literature.

claims.claim: A stretched lobe can shrink back on its own if jewelry is removed
claims.believers: Piercing communities say massage and time can help a stretched hole shrink back.[12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that shrinkage varies by person, that every stretch should be treated as permanent, and that surgical repair is the only reliable way to fully close a heavily stretched lobe.[12]

claims.claim: Torn lobes can be repaired and repierced
claims.believers: Cosmetic surgeons describe repair with immediate or later repiercing as a routine request.[3]
claims.experts: Technique papers describe Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap and double-flap closures; the main reported issue is rim notching, and no randomized trials were found.[5][6][7][8]

claims.claim: The lobe edge shows a scar or notch unless the closure is designed to avoid a straight line
claims.believers: Surgeons who published V-flap and double-flap methods say their designs prevent notching.[7][8]
claims.experts: A 1990 series reported moderate notching in simple repairs and slight notching in one of nine L-plasty repairs.[6]

claims.claim: Heavy earrings will eventually tear the lobe
claims.believers: Wearers and body-modification writers note that lobes have limits.
claims.experts: Wikipedia says a lobe can only carry so much weight, and cites about 2.5 percent traumatic tearing in one study of people with pierced ears.[13]

claims.claim: Repair is risk-free for people who scar easily
claims.believers: Some patients expect a flat scar after surgery.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that ear piercings are a common keloid site and that excision alone has a high reported recurrence rate.[14]

claims.claim: A protruding lobe can be pulled in during ear surgery
claims.believers: Otoplasty patients seek proportionate lobes alongside ear pinning.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes the Gosain technique as the method it calls most effective for repositioning the lobe, and calls repositioning the hardest part of otoplasty.[1]

card.summary: Minor plastic surgery to mend torn or split earlobes or reduce large ones; many technique papers, small case series.
card.note: Notching of the lobe edge is the outcome technique papers aim to avoid.

quick.overview:
Earlobe repair mends torn or split lobes, often from heavy earrings or stretched piercings; reduction shrinks or repositions large lobes.

The literature is mostly small technique series.
quick.mechanism: Surgeons excise scar or excess tissue and close with Z-plasty, L-plasty, V-flap or double-flap designs to prevent notching.
quick.risks: Reported issues include notching at the lobe rim; one L-plasty series reported no complications. Larger controlled studies were not found.

chain: Torn, split or enlarged lobe is excised and reshaped
Edges are closed with a notch-avoiding design
Intact, proportionate lobe, with repiercing possible later
angle.text: The surgeon removes scar or excess lobe tissue and reconstructs the rim, so the lobe looks whole again or is smaller and sits closer to the head. People seek it after torn or stretched piercings, or when a large or protruding lobule bothers them.
